title: Young black listeners and the mixed white and black record collection
summary: Tate says black kids of the 1920s listened to Bessie Smith and white bands alike and never thought of jazz as only black music.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Would it have been unusual for him to run into some young black kids who knew his records at that time?

You know, I don't think so. I think they were more turned on than today to jazz, more young black kids were turned on to jazz then because they didn't have the disco. You either liked blues singers and jazz and, you know, singers like Bessie Smith, blues singers, Mamie Smith, they were the blues singers. Then there were a lot of blacks even turned on to Gene Austin, who -- I think he sold more -- nobody's ever topped his "Blue Heaven," I don't think. I think every home in America had his "Blue Heaven." You remember that?

And then he made many songs. My mother had everything he made. And I think more black kids were turned on to jazz than they -- I don't think it would be any use because they knew about Frankie Trumbauer.
What interests me is that you were listening to whoever you liked then, it was white and black.
You didn't think of jazz as -- people didn't think of jazz as black music.
No, I didn't. We didn't. And -- oh, no, we never did. I mean, if it was good, we listened to it and we copied off the records, you know what I mean? Because we
copied off Coon-Saunders and Ted Weems and there was another band. I'm trying to think -- oh, Isham Jones. I loved Isham Jones' band, too. He had a good band.
